analysis.one_liner: Lets banks combine with securities firms and insurers, repealing the Glass-Steagall separation.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in House committee without a vote, but Congress passed a similar repeal of the Glass-Steagall banking-securities separation later that same year.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal two Depression-era Glass-Steagall provisions that barred banks from owning or affiliating with securities firms, so that a bank holding company could lend, underwrite securities, sell insurance, and give investment advice all under one roof [S2] [S3]. It would let a bank holding company start any activity the Federal Reserve deems "financial in nature" without prior approval, and it would block states from restricting banks from having insurance affiliates [S3]. It would also sharply limit the Federal Reserve's power over the new securities and insurance subsidiaries: no Fed capital requirements if another regulator already sets capital, no Fed order forcing an insurance or securities affiliate to prop up a troubled bank if that affiliate's own regulator objects, and no Fed action at all against those affiliates unless necessary to prevent material risk to a bank or the payment system [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies gain the most: they could merge banking, securities underwriting, merchant banking, and insurance into single conglomerates, start new activities with only 30 days' notice to the Fed instead of prior approval, and operate behind rules that shield their securities and insurance affiliates from Fed supervision and from state insurance restrictions [S3]. Securities firms gain access to bank capital and deposit funding; insurers gain a channel into bank holding company structures [S3]. Consumers would get some convenience from one-stop financial shopping.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Glass-Steagall Sections 20 and 32, which prohibited bank affiliation with securities firms and the sharing of personnel between them, allowing full bank-securities combinations [S3].

Lets a bank holding company engage in any activity the Federal Reserve deems financial in nature or incidental to it — including lending, insuring, financial advisory services, and securities underwriting — and to begin such activities without prior Fed approval, merely notifying the Fed within 30 days afterward [S3].
Creates a merchant-banking pathway letting bank holding company securities affiliates take ownership stakes in nonfinancial companies for appreciation and resale [S3].

Shields bank holding companies from any state law that restricts a bank from having an insurance affiliate, agent, or employee licensed in that state, and makes selling insurance as principal, agent, or broker a federally protected "financial" activity [S3].

Bars the Federal Reserve from imposing capital requirements on a non-depository subsidiary that complies with SEC or state insurance capital rules or is registered as an investment adviser, and restricts Fed examinations of such subsidiaries to cases where they pose a material risk to an affiliated bank [S3].

Makes any Fed order requiring an insurance company or securities broker-dealer affiliate to provide assets to a struggling insured bank unenforceable if that affiliate's own regulator (state insurance authority or the SEC) says in writing that doing so would materially hurt the affiliate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depositors and the federal deposit insurance fund would bear the added risk of insured deposits being tied to securities underwriting, merchant banking, and insurance ventures, while the Fed's authority to intervene early against risky affiliates is stripped back [S3]. Taxpayers stand behind insured deposits. Independent insurance agents and small financial firms would face new competition from bank-affiliated conglomerates, and state regulators would lose authority over bank insurance activities [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill dismantles the legal wall between government-insured deposits and securities speculation, allowing bank conglomerates to underwrite securities and take merchant-banking positions while deposit insurance and taxpayer backstops remain in place [S3].

It hobbles the regulator with the deepest view of bank conglomerates: the Fed could not act against securities, insurance, or investment-company affiliates unless necessary to prevent material risk to an affiliated bank or the payment system, and could not act indirectly through the holding company either [S3].

It lets a securities or insurance affiliate refuse to support its affiliated bank in a crisis if the SEC or a state insurance regulator objects, leaving the bank — and its insured depositors — exposed while the affiliate is protected [S3].
It preempts state insurance laws restricting bank insurance affiliations, reducing state-level consumer oversight of bank sales of insurance [S3].

The good-faith case for it: the separations had grown outdated as financial firms competed globally and customers wanted one-stop services, and the Fed would retain authority over bank holding companies themselves and over anything materially threatening a bank [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer convenience of buying banking, insurance, and investments from one firm is real but modest, and it was achievable under narrower reforms. The bill's center of gravity is different: it removes the firewall between insured deposits and securities risk while simultaneously cutting back the Federal Reserve's ability to police the new affiliates, pre-position capital at them, or force them to rescue a troubled bank. Weighing those honestly, the design favors consolidation and flexibility for large financial conglomerates over the safety of the deposit system; the absence of any cosponsors suggests other members of the House did not find the deregulation-vs-supervision tradeoff in this draft worth attaching their names to [S4]. Versions of the same core idea — repealing the Glass-Steagall separations — did become law that year through a separate, broader bill, so the policy question was not hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a markup or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended; a separate, broader financial-deregulation law repealing Glass-Steagall (Gramm-Leach-Bliley) was signed in November 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Baker, a Louisiana Republican, introduced the bill on February 24, 1999 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Commerce Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On March 11, 1999 it was referred to the Finance and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee, the last action recorded before the Congress ended [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in either party [S4].
The subcommittee and committee never acted, and the bill never came to a House vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large bank holding companies. Not because this bill moved — it died with no cosponsors — but because Congress passed and the President signed a broader financial deregulation law (Gramm-Leach-Bliley) in late 1999 that enacted the same central change, repealing the Glass-Steagall separation between banking and securities. The concentrated interests this bill was written for got the outcome through another vehicle within the same Congress; the deposit-insurance and supervisory questions it raised were resolved on similar terms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks, via a later similar law

for.name: Richard H. Baker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Banking and Commerce committees, where he sat; it drew no cosponsors and never reached a vote.

against.name: Jim Leach
against.role: Chair, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup; the committee instead worked a competing financial-modernization bill that became law that year.

sides.party_line_note: No votes are on record; the sole sponsor was a Republican and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to let bank conglomerates merge banking with securities underwriting, merchant banking, and insurance, and to shield those new affiliates from Federal Reserve capital rules, examinations, and enforcement unless they directly threaten a bank [S3]. The gain comes from removing the firewall that separates insured deposits from securities risk, which is the public's main protection in this area [S3].

Securities firms could affiliate with banks, gaining access to bank capital and insured deposits, and bank securities affiliates could do merchant banking — taking ownership stakes in companies for resale [S3]. Their gain is expanded consolidation financed partly by the deposit system.

Insurers gain a route into bank holding company structures, and bank sales of insurance are made a protected federal activity, but the same provision preempts state restrictions on bank insurance affiliations, weakening the state oversight that governs insurers and agents alike [S3].

industries.industry: Independent insurance agents and small financial firms
industries.note: Bank holding companies would sell insurance as principal, agent, or broker nationwide, overriding state affiliation restrictions, so independent agents and smaller firms face new competition from bank-owned conglomerates [S3].

The bill shields bank holding companies from any state law restricting bank insurance affiliates and shifts interpretive and enforcement authority over insurance activities to state authorities in a deference scheme the Fed must follow [S2] [S3].
